results.content:
Title: Multi-GPU training ⚡Lightning AI - Docs
# Multi-GPU training. Multi-GPU training enables massive speed ups to model training. As a general guideline, doubling the GPUs halves the training time. For example, if a model trains in 24 hours on 1 GPU you can expect it to take 12 hours on 2 GPUs or 6 hours on 4 GPUs. Achieving such linear speed-ups requires a LOT of effort. Tools like PyTorch Lightning and Studios are here to simplify the process by handling distribution efficiently. Scale your training to multi-GPU. Start a Studio and change to 4 GPUs. https://pl-bolts-doc-images.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/Docs\_Studios\_MP4/Docs\_TrainModels\_SwitchToMultiGPU.mp4. ## PyTorch Lightning multi-GPU. These tools automatically detect the 4 GPUs. There are zero code changes required. Use PyTorch Lightning or Lightning Fabric to switch machines with no code changes! ## PyTorch multi-GPU. Running on multiple GPUs without PyTorch Lightning takes a significant amount of work. However, if you are confident you have handled these considerations, the Studio provides useful environment variables for your setup. Here's how you might set up the distributed environment for PyTorch:. We recommend you look into Fabric or PyTorch Lightning which handles all other training logistics for you. To use multiple GPUs with other frameworks, refer to the documentation of the framework which usually requires a few environment variables available on the Studio:. We recommend you look into Fabric or PyTorch Lightning which handles all other training logistics for you. A key objective in multi-GPU setups is linear performance scaling. Using a single T4 GPU instance costs $0.68 per hour, compared to $3.39 per hour for an instance with four T4 GPUs. **Ideally**, the cost **doesn't increase** with more GPUs if linear scaling is achieved. These tips can save you around 60% in development costs and make your development process 6x faster. ## Develop on CPU, run on GPU. This creates a lot of wasted time and GPU hours on inefficient GPU usage. Once you're confident, switch to a cheap GPU. Once that's done, switch to a multi-GPU Studio and run your code again. If your ML framework does not support changing hardware without code changes, then consider using PyTorch Lightning to pretrain or finetune your model. Now switch to 1 GPU and run the code again.

results.title: How long should I run spacy pretrain for? - usage - Prodigy Support
results.content:
Title: How long should I run spacy pretrain for? - usage - Prodigy Support
# How long should I run spacy pretrain for? I've been running spacy pretrain for around 16 hours at this point (on an AWS p3.2xlarge instance with a large Tesla V100 GPU). There should be a `log.jsonl` that provides an `epoch_loss`, which makes it easier to see whether it's still learning. Btw I've been trying to developI some improvements to the pretraining myself at the moment. If you don't mind that your models will be a bit slower on CPU, and you have a lot of text to pretrain with, you can try setting the width to 300, depth to 8, and the embedding rows to 20k. The pretrain arguments are: `-er 20000 -cw 300 -cd 8`, while the `spacy train` environment variables would be `embed_size=20000 token_vector_width=300 conv_depth=8` (we're working on fixing the pretty terrible hyper-parameter configuration stuff). The v2.1 models set this a bit too low, especially for pretraining. The Tesla V100 I am using (16GB GPU memory) seems to run out of memory when I specify the full set of hyperparameters recommended:. `$> spacy pretrain tasks/all.jsonl en_core_web_lg ./models/pretrain/v0.2/temp/ -er 20000 -cw 300 -cd 8. File "cupy/cuda/memory.pyx", line 734, in cupy.cuda.memory._try_malloc. However, if I drop the "-cw 300 -cd 8" and only specify the "-er 20000" then pretrain seems to have started...
